prompt: Which of these does each thread in a process get **its own copy** of?

options.text: The heap
options.explanation: The heap is shared: memory one thread allocates with `malloc` (or any Python object it creates) is visible to every thread that has a pointer to it.

options.text: Global variables
options.explanation: Globals live in the process's data segment, which all threads share. That is exactly why unprotected globals cause races.

options.text: The table of open file descriptors
options.explanation: File descriptors belong to the process. If one thread opens a file, another thread can read from that descriptor, and closing it closes it for all.

options.text: The stack
options.explanation: Correct. Each thread has its own stack holding its local variables and return addresses, because each thread is at a different point in its own chain of function calls.

prompt: Select **all** of the following that are shared by every thread of a single process.

options.text: Objects allocated on the heap
options.explanation: Correct. There is one heap per process; any thread holding a pointer or reference can use the object.

options.text: Open file descriptors
options.explanation: Correct. The file descriptor table belongs to the process (on Linux, threads are created with `CLONE_FILES`).

options.text: The program counter
options.explanation: Wrong: each thread is at its own point in the code, so each has its own program counter. Sharing it would mean they were one thread.

options.text: Global variables
options.explanation: Correct. Globals live in the shared data segment, which is why they need protection when several threads write them.

options.text: The CPU registers
options.explanation: Wrong: registers are part of each thread's private execution context; the kernel saves and restores them on every switch.

workedExample:
Sort each item into "process resource" or "execution context":

| Item | Belongs to |
|---|---|
| Heap | Process (shared) |
| File descriptors | Process (shared) |
| Globals | Process (shared) |
| Program counter | Thread (private) |
| Registers | Thread (private) |

The execution context (PC, registers, stack) is what makes a thread a thread. Everything else is shared.

options.text: `mine=1`, `mine=2`, `mine=3` in some order
options.explanation: This would be true only if `mine` were shared. It is a local variable, so each thread has its own copy on its own stack.

options.text: `mine=1` three times
options.explanation: Correct. `mine` lives on each thread's private stack, starts at 0 and is incremented once, so every thread prints 1. It is `hits` that is shared.

options.text: `mine=3` three times
options.explanation: That assumes all three increments land on the same variable before anyone prints. Locals are per thread, so no thread ever sees another's increment.

options.text: It is unpredictable because of a data race on `mine`
options.explanation: There is no race on `mine`, and the shared `hits` update uses an atomic operation. Each call prints its own `mine` value.

workedExample: Each call has its own automatic `mine` variable, increments it from 0 to 1 and prints `mine=1`. The shared `hits` counter is now atomic, so three completed calls increment it to 3 without a data race. The original non-atomic `hits++` would make the entire C program undefined, even though `mine` itself was not shared.

prompt: Select **all** correct reasons why switching between two threads of the **same** process is usually cheaper than switching between two different processes.

options.text: The page tables stay the same, so there is no address-space switch
options.explanation: Correct. Both threads use the same address space, so the kernel doesn't load a new page-table root.

options.text: Cached address translations in the TLB stay valid
options.explanation: Correct. Because the address space doesn't change, the TLB entries still apply, avoiding a burst of TLB misses afterwards.

options.text: Threads don't have registers that need saving
options.explanation: Wrong: every thread has its own registers and the kernel must save and restore them on each switch, just as for processes.

options.text: The kernel is not involved in switching between kernel threads
options.explanation: Wrong: kernel threads are scheduled by the kernel, so a switch still involves entering the kernel. Only user-level threads avoid it.

options.text: The CPU caches are more likely to hold useful data
options.explanation: Correct. The threads share code and often data, so the incoming thread may find some of its working set already in cache.

workedExample: Both cases save/restore thread state. Sharing an address space can avoid changing memory maps, and shared code/data can preserve useful locality. Translation validity is not guaranteed cache residency; PCID can preserve process translations too. These are possible savings, not a universal ordering of measured switch latency.

prompt: A worker in a 50-thread process incurs a memory fault that generates SIGSEGV, with its default terminating disposition unchanged. What happens?

options.text: The whole process, including all 50 threads, is killed
options.explanation: Correct. Threads share one address space and one set of signal dispositions, so a fatal signal in any thread terminates the entire process.

options.text: Only that worker thread dies; the other 49 keep serving
options.explanation: That is the isolation processes give you, not threads. A SIGSEGV's default action terminates the whole process.

options.text: The thread is restarted automatically by the threads library
options.explanation: pthreads has no supervisor that restarts crashed threads. The default action for SIGSEGV kills the process.

options.text: Nothing, because each thread has its own private memory
options.explanation: Threads share memory; only their stacks are separate, and even those aren't protected. A NULL dereference raises SIGSEGV for the process.

workedExample: SIGSEGV with its ordinary default action terminates the process, ending all 50 threads. Separate processes provide a memory-isolation boundary, but shared resources and recovery policy can still couple failures; a worker crash does not guarantee that every other service process continues uninterrupted.
